summary:
Tula Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the sources reviewed identify no deviation from that position material enough to assess separately. For a trans visitor the national position means that same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect.

The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation and the expanded "propaganda" law apply in Tula Oblast as they apply in every other region. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised, but public expression is: the 2013 propaganda statute carries administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is documented at volume. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement volume has risen sharply. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian documented the speed of the post-designation crackdown on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside the legal regime. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tula Oblast have no domestic route to legal gender recognition: gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited and the procedures for legal gender change were removed alongside the ban on gender reassignment surgery in 2023. Gender-affirming medical care is unavailable under law.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. The same note assesses that the state is able but unwilling to protect openly LGBT+ people from societal discrimination that may amount to persecution.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) called on governments to offer safe haven to people leaving Russia over the extremist designation and the surrounding enforcement wave.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tula Oblast-specific reporting on policing practice, healthcare availability, documentation processing or incidents involving transgender residents was located in the sources reviewed; whether local enforcement diverges from the national pattern is unresolved.

The source inventory supplies conviction and charge totals at the national level only. Distribution of the 101 extremism-related convictions by region, and any figure specific to Tula Oblast, is not sourced here.

Figures on the total number of people affected by anti-LGBT+ laws derive from a single UK Home Office count covering 2022 to 2024; no independent corroboration or more recent total appears in the inventory.
